title: Persuasion Techniques
subtitle: Structure a formal argument, deploy rhetorical devices, and answer objections with tact

lessons.title: Structurer un argumentaire
lessons.description: Build a formal argument that moves cleanly from thesis to evidence, counter-argument, and conclusion.

blocks.heading: La thèse : annoncer sa position
blocks.body: A formal French argument ('un argumentaire') opens by stating 'la thèse' — the single claim everything else will support. State it early, in one clear sentence, before any evidence appears; French readers expect to know your position before they read your reasons. Avoid hedging in the thesis itself ('on pourrait peut-être penser que...'); save nuance for later and let the opening sentence be direct.

examples.french: Ma thèse est simple : ce projet coûte plus qu'il ne rapporte.
examples.english: My thesis is simple: this project costs more than it brings in.

examples.french: Je soutiens que le télétravail améliore la productivité à long terme.
examples.english: I maintain that remote work improves productivity in the long run.

examples.french: Cet argumentaire défend une idée centrale : la formation continue doit être obligatoire.
examples.english: This argument defends one central idea: ongoing training should be mandatory.

examples.french: D'entrée de jeu, précisons notre position sur cette réforme.
examples.english: From the outset, let's make our position on this reform clear.

examples.french: Contrairement à une idée reçue, cette mesure profite surtout aux petites entreprises.
examples.english: Contrary to popular belief, this measure mainly benefits small businesses.

blocks.tip: Underline your thesis mentally as you write it — every later paragraph should point back to that one sentence, never wander off it.

blocks.heading: Les preuves et le contre-argument
blocks.body: Once the thesis is stated, 'le développement' supplies 'des preuves' — facts, statistics, or examples — each introduced by a connector such as 'd'abord', 'ensuite', or 'de plus'. A B2-level argument then does something weaker writers skip: it names 'le contre-argument' honestly, using 'cependant' or 'en revanche', before showing why the thesis still stands. Conceding a real weakness briefly, then answering it, reads as more convincing than ignoring it.

examples.french: D'abord, les chiffres de l'INSEE confirment cette tendance depuis dix ans.
examples.english: First, INSEE figures confirm this trend over the past ten years.

examples.french: De plus, plusieurs entreprises pilotes ont déjà constaté les mêmes résultats.
examples.english: What is more, several pilot companies have already observed the same results.

examples.french: Certains objecteront que le coût initial reste élevé.
examples.english: Some will object that the initial cost remains high.

examples.french: Cependant, cet investissement s'amortit en moins de deux ans.
examples.english: However, this investment pays for itself in under two years.

examples.french: On pourrait croire que cette mesure ne touche que les grandes villes ; en réalité, elle concerne tout le territoire.
examples.english: One might think this measure only affects big cities; in reality, it concerns the whole country.

blocks.tip: Naming the counter-argument yourself, before an opponent does, is a classic move in French formal debate — it signals you have thought the issue through.

blocks.heading: La conclusion : boucler l'argumentaire
blocks.body: 'La conclusion' does not introduce new evidence; it restates the thesis in a fresh sentence and shows, in one or two lines, why the evidence just given supports it. French formal writing favours a closing connector — 'en conclusion', 'pour conclure', 'en somme' — so the reader hears the argument end rather than simply stop. A strong conclusion often ends on a slightly wider note: a consequence, a recommendation, or a question that lingers.

examples.french: En conclusion, les avantages l'emportent nettement sur les inconvénients.
examples.english: In conclusion, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

examples.french: Pour conclure, cette réforme mérite d'être testée à plus grande échelle.
examples.english: To conclude, this reform deserves to be tested on a larger scale.

examples.french: En somme, l'argumentaire repose sur des faits vérifiables, pas sur des impressions.
examples.english: In short, the argument rests on verifiable facts, not on impressions.

examples.french: Ainsi, la question n'est plus de savoir si, mais quand appliquer cette mesure.
examples.english: Thus, the question is no longer whether, but when to apply this measure.

examples.french: Par conséquent, il paraît raisonnable d'adopter cette proposition dès la rentrée.
examples.english: Consequently, it seems reasonable to adopt this proposal starting in the autumn.

blocks.tip: Never end on the counter-argument — always give the thesis the last word.

items.exampleEnglish: Finally, the conclusion restates the thesis in one strong sentence.

blocks.heading: Les connecteurs logiques d'un argumentaire
blocks.body: French formal argument leans on a fixed toolkit of connectors, grouped by function: sequence ('d'abord', 'ensuite', 'enfin'), addition ('de plus', 'par ailleurs'), opposition ('cependant', 'en revanche', 'néanmoins'), and consequence ('par conséquent', 'ainsi'). Using one from each group, in that rough order, is what makes a paragraph read as reasoned rather than as a list of loose sentences. Mixing an addition connector where an opposition one belongs is a common, jarring B2 mistake — check that the connector actually matches the logical move you are making.

examples.french: D'abord, la mesure réduit les coûts ; ensuite, elle simplifie les démarches.
examples.english: First, the measure reduces costs; then, it simplifies procedures.

examples.french: De plus, elle bénéficie d'un large soutien parmi les employés.
examples.english: What is more, it enjoys wide support among employees.

examples.french: Cependant, sa mise en place demande une formation initiale.
examples.english: However, putting it in place requires initial training.

examples.french: Par conséquent, un budget de transition semble indispensable.
examples.english: Consequently, a transition budget seems essential.

blocks.tip: Read your paragraph aloud and check each connector: does it really add, oppose, or conclude — or did you pick it just for variety?

blocks.heading: Exprimer la nécessité : il est essentiel de / que
blocks.body: Formal argument often states what must be done rather than what merely happens, using impersonal structures: 'il est essentiel de' + infinitive (same subject as the sentence) or 'il est essentiel que' + subjunctive (different subject introduced). The same pattern works with 'il convient de/que', 'il importe de/que', and 'il faut que'. Choosing the infinitive or the subjunctive is not free variation — it depends on whether a new subject is named after 'que'.

examples.french: Il est essentiel de présenter des preuves concrètes.
examples.english: It is essential to present concrete evidence.

examples.french: Il est essentiel que le lecteur comprenne la thèse dès la première ligne.
examples.english: It is essential that the reader understand the thesis from the first line.

examples.french: Il convient de traiter le contre-argument avant de conclure.
examples.english: It is fitting to address the counter-argument before concluding.

examples.french: Il importe que chaque idée soit illustrée par un exemple.
examples.english: It matters that every idea be illustrated with an example.

blocks.tip: No new subject after 'que' → use the infinitive form ('il est essentiel de + verb'); a new subject appears → switch to the subjunctive.

items.prompt: Name a counter-argument, then dismiss it with 'cependant'.

passages.title: Le conseil municipal
passages.french:
Le mardi soir, la salle du conseil municipal est pleine à craquer.
Camille, étudiante en droit, prend la parole pour la première fois.
— Ma thèse est simple : notre quartier a besoin d'une piste cyclable sécurisée.
Elle marque une pause, puis reprend d'une voix posée.
— D'abord, le nombre d'accidents impliquant des cyclistes a doublé en trois ans.
— Ensuite, une étude de la mairie de Lyon montre qu'une piste réduit ce chiffre de moitié.
— De plus, les commerçants du quartier soutiennent le projet : ils espèrent plus de clients à vélo.
Un conseiller lève la main.
— Certains objecteront que les travaux coûteront cher et dureront plusieurs mois.
Camille hoche la tête, sans se démonter.
— Cependant, une subvention régionale couvrirait soixante pour cent du budget.
— En revanche, retarder ce projet coûterait plus cher encore, en accidents évités.
Elle conclut d'une phrase ferme.
— En conclusion, cette piste cyclable profite à tous : cyclistes, commerçants, et riverains.
Le président du conseil la remercie chaleureusement pour cet argumentaire limpide.
passages.english:
On Tuesday evening, the council chamber is packed.
Camille, a law student, speaks for the first time.
— My thesis is simple: our neighbourhood needs a safe cycle path.
She pauses, then continues in a steady voice.
— First, the number of accidents involving cyclists has doubled in three years.
— Next, a study by the city of Lyon shows that a cycle path cuts that number in half.
— What is more, local shopkeepers support the project: they expect more customers on bikes.
A council member raises his hand.
— Some will object that the works will be expensive and last several months.
Camille nods, unfazed.
— However, a regional grant would cover sixty percent of the budget.
— On the other hand, delaying this project would cost even more, in accidents that could have been avoided.
She closes with one firm sentence.
— In conclusion, this cycle path benefits everyone: cyclists, shopkeepers, and residents alike.
The council chair thanks her warmly for such a clear argument.

lessons.title: Les figures de l'argumentation
lessons.description: Recognise and use rhetorical devices — rhetorical question, anaphora, gradation — that make a speech memorable and persuasive.

blocks.heading: La question rhétorique
blocks.body: 'La question rhétorique' is asked without expecting an answer — the answer is already obvious to the audience, and the question exists to make them arrive at it themselves. In formal French speech, it usually appears at a turning point in the argument, right after the evidence, so that the audience answers 'yes, of course' in their own heads before the speaker moves on. Overusing it flattens the effect, so B2 speakers reserve it for a single decisive moment.

examples.french: Qui accepterait de perdre son emploi sans réagir ?
examples.english: Who would accept losing their job without reacting?

examples.french: Comment rester silencieux face à des chiffres aussi alarmants ?
examples.english: How can one stay silent in the face of such alarming figures?

examples.french: Faut-il rappeler que ce projet a déjà fait ses preuves ailleurs ?
examples.english: Need we recall that this project has already proven itself elsewhere?

examples.french: N'est-il pas temps d'agir, plutôt que d'attendre encore ?
examples.english: Is it not time to act, rather than wait any longer?

examples.french: Qui, sincèrement, peut croire que rien ne changera ?
examples.english: Who, honestly, can believe that nothing will change?

blocks.tip: A rhetorical question works best right after a fact, not before it — let the evidence do the convincing, then let the question seal it.

blocks.heading: L'anaphore : répéter pour marquer les esprits
blocks.body: 'L'anaphore' repeats the same word or phrase at the start of consecutive sentences or clauses. It builds rhythm, and rhythm is what an audience remembers after the exact words are forgotten. Political and union speeches use it constantly in French; in an everyday argument, three repetitions is usually the natural limit — a fourth starts to sound like a chant rather than an argument.

examples.french: Nous voulons plus de moyens. Nous voulons plus de temps. Nous voulons être entendus.
examples.english: We want more resources. We want more time. We want to be heard.

examples.french: Jamais nous n'avons reculé. Jamais nous n'avons cédé.
examples.english: Never have we backed down. Never have we given in.

examples.french: Ce projet, c'est de l'emploi. Ce projet, c'est de l'avenir.
examples.english: This project means jobs. This project means the future.

examples.french: Chaque jour compte. Chaque décision compte.
examples.english: Every day counts. Every decision counts.

blocks.tip: Say the repeated word with the exact same stress each time — a flat, mechanical repetition is what gives anaphora its force.

blocks.heading: La gradation : monter en intensité
blocks.body: 'La gradation' lines up words or clauses in rising (or falling) order of intensity, so the sentence itself seems to build toward a climax. In French it often takes the form of a short list of three or four terms, each stronger than the last, sometimes without a connector between them — the accumulation does the work. It pairs naturally with the rhetorical question or the anaphora as the final push of an argument.

examples.french: Difficile, puis impossible, puis absurde.
examples.english: Difficult, then impossible, then absurd.

examples.french: Il n'a pas seulement protesté : il a résisté, il s'est battu, il a gagné.
examples.english: He didn't just protest: he resisted, he fought, he won.

examples.french: Ce n'est plus un problème, c'est une crise, c'est une urgence.
examples.english: This is no longer a problem, it's a crisis, it's an emergency.

examples.french: Outragé, brisé, mais debout.
examples.english: Outraged, broken, but still standing.

blocks.tip: Read a gradation with an increasing volume or pace across the list — the delivery should physically climb along with the words.

blocks.heading: L'inversion sujet-verbe dans la question rhétorique
blocks.body: Formal rhetorical questions favour subject-verb inversion ('Faut-il rappeler...' rather than 'Est-ce qu'il faut rappeler...') because inversion sounds more literary and more forceful in spoken argument. With a noun subject, French keeps the noun in place and adds a pronoun after the verb: 'Le public accepte-t-il...?' A negative rhetorical question ('N'est-il pas temps...?') is especially common, since it invites the single obvious answer 'yes' even more strongly than a plain question would.

examples.french: Faut-il rappeler que ce projet a déjà fait ses preuves ?

blocks.tip: Add '-t-' between the verb and the pronoun when the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun starts with one: 'parle-t-il', never 'parle-il'.

blocks.heading: Construire une gradation : l'accumulation sans connecteur
blocks.body: A gradation usually drops the connectors a plain list would need ('d'abord', 'puis') in favour of commas alone, letting the accumulation itself carry the rising energy: 'Difficile, puis impossible, puis absurde' already climbs without 'et'. Verbs in a gradation are often repeated in the same tense and person, reinforcing the parallel structure that makes the climax land. Three steps is the classic minimum; four is common; beyond that, the device starts to lose its punch.

examples.french: Il n'a pas seulement protesté : il a résisté, il s'est battu, il a gagné.
examples.english: He didn't just protest: he resisted, he fought, he won.

blocks.tip: Keep every term in a gradation the same grammatical form (all verbs, all adjectives, all short clauses) — mixing forms breaks the climb.

passages.title: Le discours de Lina
passages.french:
Lina répète son discours pour la troisième fois devant le miroir.
Demain, elle doit convaincre le conseil des élèves de financer un jardin partagé.
Elle commence doucement, puis sa voix se raffermit.
— Qui, parmi nous, n'a jamais rêvé d'un coin de verdure dans cette cour de béton ?
Sa question rhétorique reste suspendue quelques secondes.
— Ce jardin, c'est de l'air pur. Ce jardin, c'est du lien entre les classes. Ce jardin, c'est notre fierté.
L'anaphore résonne, et déjà certains élèves hochent la tête.
Puis elle enchaîne sur une gradation soigneusement préparée.
— Ce n'est plus une idée, c'est un projet, c'est une nécessité.
Son professeur, au fond de la salle, sourit en reconnaissant la figure de style.
— N'est-il pas temps de transformer nos discours en actes ?
Elle termine sur cette dernière question, sans laisser le silence retomber.
Le lendemain, devant le vrai conseil, Lina reprend exactement les mêmes mots.
Cette fois, l'auditoire applaudit avant même qu'elle ait terminé.
passages.english:
Lina rehearses her speech for the third time in front of the mirror.
Tomorrow, she has to convince the student council to fund a shared garden.
She starts softly, then her voice grows steadier.
— Which of us has never dreamed of a patch of greenery in this concrete yard?
Her rhetorical question hangs in the air for a few seconds.
— This garden means clean air. This garden means a bond between classes. This garden means our pride.
The anaphora resonates, and some students are already nodding.
Then she moves into a carefully prepared gradation.
— This is no longer an idea, it's a project, it's a necessity.
Her teacher, at the back of the room, smiles as he recognises the device.
— Is it not time to turn our words into actions?
She ends on this final question, without letting the silence settle.
The next day, in front of the real council, Lina repeats the exact same words.
This time, the audience applauds before she has even finished.

lessons.title: Répondre aux objections
lessons.description: Handle disagreement diplomatically: acknowledge an objection, concede what is fair, and steer the discussion toward common ground.

blocks.heading: Accueillir l'objection avec tact
blocks.body: In French formal exchange, the first move against an objection is not to answer it but to acknowledge it — a brief phrase showing you heard and respect the concern before you say anything else. Skipping this step, even to give a perfectly correct answer, tends to read as dismissive. 'Je comprends votre inquiétude', 'C'est une remarque intéressante', or simply 'Je vous entends' buy the goodwill needed for the rest of the response to land.

examples.french: Je comprends votre inquiétude concernant le budget.
examples.english: I understand your concern about the budget.

examples.french: C'est une remarque tout à fait légitime.
examples.english: That is a completely legitimate remark.

examples.french: Merci de le souligner, c'est un point important.
examples.english: Thank you for pointing that out, it's an important point.

examples.french: Je vous entends, et je comprends que ce délai inquiète.
examples.english: I hear you, and I understand that this deadline is worrying.

examples.french: Votre objection mérite qu'on s'y arrête un instant.
examples.english: Your objection deserves a moment's attention.

blocks.tip: Never follow an acknowledgement with 'mais' too abruptly — a short pause or a connector like 'cela dit' softens the turn toward your answer.

blocks.heading: Concéder puis répondre : certes... mais
blocks.body: The classic diplomatic pattern is 'certes... mais' (or 'bien que'/'quoique' + subjunctive): grant that part of the objection is true, then pivot to why your position still holds. This is different from simply disagreeing — a real concession names a specific point the other person is right about, rather than a vague 'yes, but' that concedes nothing. 'Bien que' and 'quoique' both take the subjunctive and place the concession in a subordinate clause, which reads as more formal than 'certes'.

examples.french: Certes, le délai est court, mais il reste réalisable.
examples.english: Admittedly, the deadline is short, but it remains achievable.

examples.french: Bien que votre objection soit fondée, la solution reste la même.
examples.english: Although your objection is well founded, the solution remains the same.

examples.french: Quoique je comprenne votre inquiétude, les chiffres sont clairs.
examples.english: Although I understand your concern, the figures are clear.

examples.french: Il est vrai que le coût est élevé ; cela dit, le retour sur investissement l'est aussi.
examples.english: It is true that the cost is high; that said, so is the return on investment.

examples.french: Je concède que votre remarque n'est pas sans fondement.
examples.english: I concede that your remark is not without foundation.

blocks.tip: Name the exact point you are conceding — a vague concession sounds evasive, a precise one sounds honest.

blocks.heading: Désamorcer et proposer un compromis
blocks.body: Once the objection is acknowledged and partly conceded, French diplomatic register moves toward common ground rather than toward victory: clarifying a possible misunderstanding, reformulating the disagreement in neutral terms, and proposing a concrete compromise. Ending on 'un terrain d'entente' rather than on who was right keeps the relationship intact — often more valuable, in a professional setting, than winning the specific point.

blocks.heading: Bien que / quoique + subjonctif
blocks.body: 'Bien que' and 'quoique' both introduce a concession and both require the subjunctive in the clause that follows, even though the fact conceded is real and true — the subjunctive here signals a concession, not doubt about the fact itself. Word order is flexible: the concessive clause can open the sentence ('Bien que le délai soit court, ...') or follow the main clause. Both conjunctions are interchangeable in meaning; 'quoique' is slightly more literary.

examples.french: Bien que votre objection soit fondée, la solution reste la même.
examples.english: Although your objection is well founded, the solution remains the same.

examples.french: Quoique je comprenne votre inquiétude, les chiffres sont clairs.
examples.english: Although I understand your concern, the figures are clear.

examples.french: Le projet avance, bien que certains détails restent à régler.

blocks.tip: 'Quoique' elides before a vowel ('quoiqu'il') just like 'que' — never write it as two separate words in this sense (that would be 'quoi que', meaning 'whatever').

blocks.heading: Le conditionnel pour adoucir une réponse
blocks.body: The conditional softens a diplomatic response by turning a flat statement into a tentative suggestion: 'je dirais que' instead of 'je dis que', 'il me semble que' instead of 'c'est', 'on pourrait envisager' instead of 'on va faire'. This is not about uncertainty — the speaker may be entirely sure — but about leaving the other person room to respond without feeling contradicted outright.

blocks.tip: Swap a blunt present-tense claim for its conditional cousin whenever you want to disagree without sounding like you are contradicting someone.

passages.title: La réunion d'équipe
passages.french:
Le lundi matin, Sami présente son projet de nouveaux horaires devant toute l'équipe.
À peine a-t-il terminé qu'Amina lève la main, visiblement contrariée.
— Ce nouveau planning ne tient pas compte des parents qui doivent récupérer leurs enfants à seize heures.
Sami hoche la tête avant de répondre.
— Je comprends votre inquiétude, et c'est une remarque tout à fait légitime.
— Certes, ce planning simplifie l'organisation générale, mais il ne doit pénaliser personne.
Amina croise les bras, un peu surprise par cette réponse posée.
— Il y a peut-être un malentendu, ajoute Sami : le planning reste flexible pour les parents.
— Que diriez-vous d'un compromis : les horaires fixes pour la majorité, un aménagement pour les autres ?
Un collègue approuve doucement, puis un deuxième.
— Bien que la proposition initiale semble imparfaite, cette solution convient à tout le monde, conclut Sami.
Amina sourit enfin et accepte le compromis proposé.
À la fin de la réunion, personne ne se sent ignoré ni mis de côté.
Sami note, satisfait, que l'écoute a évité un conflit inutile.
passages.english:
On Monday morning, Sami presents his new schedule project to the whole team.
He has barely finished when Amina raises her hand, clearly annoyed.
— This new schedule doesn't take into account parents who have to pick up their children at four o'clock.
Sami nods before answering.
— I understand your concern, and that's a completely legitimate remark.
— Admittedly, this schedule simplifies the overall organisation, but it must not penalise anyone.
Amina crosses her arms, a little surprised by this calm response.
— There may be a misunderstanding, Sami adds: the schedule remains flexible for parents.
— What would you say to a compromise: fixed hours for the majority, an adjustment for the others?
A colleague nods slowly in agreement, then a second one.
— Although the initial proposal seems imperfect, this solution suits everyone, Sami concludes.
Amina finally smiles and accepts the proposed compromise.
By the end of the meeting, no one feels ignored or left out.
Sami notes, satisfied, that listening avoided an unnecessary conflict.
